questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Repeated Integrals Expressed in Polar Coordinates
questions.worked_solution:
First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta $ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\frac{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}}{2}-0)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}2{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate with respect to $\theta :$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}2{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[\theta +\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )]}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2\pi )) \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Not Centered at the Origin
questions.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14067931/assets/32c4bf490df51121ddf1575df8211033185d392fd5b08519971723b820da191f.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at $(0,\frac{1}{2}).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14067931/assets/b1e2eac0041d0b0cb802561b3fb83fd8fab1b940cb6c42f698879837c06cbff0.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ (the positive $y$-axis) and $\theta =\pi $ (the negative $x$-axis):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14067931/assets/193601785ff94605d12b91b7cab1e7390af532ba1912530bd8d3f492324e2788.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Integrate the function $f(x,y)=\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}$ over the portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at the origin, where $x\le 0$ and $y\le 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14067931/assets/e4275e74a45deb22c0ed22546772e33fbd5caeb89a4036b1a2f4870e8ecf67a1.png)

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,\pi \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2}{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+1}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{{r}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡({r}^{2}+1)]_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2[\theta ]_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2(\frac{3\pi }{2}-\pi ) \\  & =\frac{\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡2}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Integrate the function $f(x,y)=4{y}^{2}$ over the disk of radius $3$ centered at the origin.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14067931/assets/0a1de805051eff4ea82b4eefb7bb113c724b3d4e7304704831b6294ee4e4d674.png)

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}4{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}4{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,{[{r}^{4}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (81-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =81{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =81{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{81}{2}{[\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{81}{2}[(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0)] \\  & =\frac{81}{2}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =81\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Not Centered at the Origin
questions.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA={∬}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14067931/assets/f0417011f46d3860b7de86fe652a7d80dd9787cb05c2057601b41c17e0c2b423.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents the disk of radius $1$ centered at $(0,1).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=1$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =1 \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)}^{2} & =1 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1 & =1 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire circle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14067931/assets/3f4bb1428a6cc9b7e191e1904636d654145d9a1f2fb1dd40843d8cd878194772.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =0$ (the positive $x$-axis) and $\theta =\pi $ (the negative $x$-axis):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14067931/assets/d6f4e054767650cd2a3d348aee8210af421e2df21792d79f42c5a58b5f4e82e6.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
